quote: Evolutionary psychology is another example of a case where rationality has to take over from science. While theories of evolutionary psychology form a connected whole, only some of those theories are readily testable experimentally. But you still need the other parts of the theory, because they form a connected web that helps you to form the hypotheses that are actually testable—and then the helper hypotheses are supported in a Bayesian sense, but not supported experimentally.
content: The example chosen to show rationality supplementing science is the field whose testable parts fared worst in the decade that followed. The “connected web” of untested ancestral-environment hypotheses is what the field’s critics call just-so stories, and the Bayesian support that the essay says flows from tested parts to untested ones flows only while the tested parts hold. Book III’s annotations recorded what happened to them: the Ekman universals, the stated mate preferences, the ovulatory-shift effects, the optimism bias and the grief-correlation study did not survive replication, sample diversification or reanalysis. When the tested nodes of a web fail, the untested nodes lose the support they were borrowing, and the essay’s “indirectly supported” verdict becomes “indirectly unsupported.” The methodological point is sound: a connected theory can be evaluated as a whole. The illustration was the wrong one, and the book’s reliance on the field, here and in Einstein’s Speed (“the most sane thinking I have seen in any scientific field”), is a case study in the risk the essay is describing.

quote: Reviving a cryonically frozen mammal is just not something you’d expect to be able to do with modern technology, even if future nanotechnologies could in fact perform a successful revival. That’s how I see Bayes seeing it.
content: The essay’s own rule is that absence of evidence counts to the degree that evidence would be expected, and it then names only the evidence that would not be expected (whole-mammal revival) and omits the evidence that would. Intermediate tests were available and have since been run: whether cryoprotectant perfusion preserves the fine structure of synapses (aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation of a rabbit brain won the Brain Preservation Prize in 2016 on that criterion, McIntyre & Fahy (2015)); whether vitrified organs recover function (a rabbit kidney, partially, Fahy et al. 2009, not since extended); and whether the protocols actually used on human patients, after hours of ischaemia and with the perfusion quality reported in case files, achieve anything like laboratory conditions (the published case reports say often not). So Bayes, seeing it, would update on the evidence that is expected and available, and it is mixed: structural preservation under ideal conditions is real, functional recovery of any brain is not, and the practice diverges from the ideal. The ambulance analogy is the wrong one, since an ambulance has a track record; the honest analogy is an experimental treatment with a mechanism and no outcomes, which is a reasonable thing to bet on and not a thing to call obviously rational.

quote: why the hell isn’t anyone testing Seth Roberts’s theory of appetite suppression?
content: Nobody tested it, and by the essay’s own principle that is informative. The Shangri-La diet (flavourless calories, oil or sugar water, taken between meals to lower a set point) was supported by Roberts’s self-experiments and by the testimonials of readers, a class of evidence the book elsewhere treats as worthless; no controlled trial was ever run, the mechanism (a Pavlovian flavour–calorie association setting body weight) was not confirmed in the obesity literature, and Roberts, who practiced his own regimen of self-experimentation for decades, died in 2014 of a cardiac condition with a coronary artery disease finding at autopsy. The essay’s general point stands: the absence of a cheap test is suspicious. Its exception for a theory the author found appealing is the pattern the book’s essays on motivated reasoning describe, and the annotator’s only addition is that “respected sources” for the anecdotes were, in this case, the readers of two blogs.
